name: The AI Enablement Audit
title: The AI Enablement Audit
answer: An AI enablement audit is a structured review of how an organization adopts, operates, and governs artificial intelligence. It covers the inventory of AI tools, the data they access, the business processes they support, and the controls around them. The audit looks at both sanctioned systems and shadow use by employees, including public chatbots and browser plugins. Its purpose is to identify where AI can be used safely and where it creates legal, security, or operational exposure. It is not a product certification or a one-time compliance check.

sections.body: An AI enablement audit is a structured review of how an organization adopts, operates, and governs artificial intelligence. It covers the inventory of AI tools, the data they access, the business processes they support, and the controls around them. The audit looks at both sanctioned systems and shadow use by employees, including public chatbots and browser plugins. Its purpose is to identify where AI can be used safely and where it creates legal, security, or operational exposure. It is not a product certification or a one-time compliance check.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on existing enterprise documentation, configuration records, access logs, and interviews with system owners. It examines the technical substrate that AI depends on, such as cloud tenants, identity providers, data warehouses, API gateways, and model endpoints. No dedicated machine learning platform is required to perform the audit, though the presence of one changes the depth of review. The auditor may use lightweight scripts to check for exposed credentials, unauthenticated endpoints, or overly broad permissions. The findings are recorded in a register that maps each risk to the underlying infrastructure component.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a combination of document review, stakeholder interviews, and targeted technical testing. The auditor maps data flows from source systems to model inputs and outputs, then compares those flows against stated policies and contractual terms. Access controls are tested against the principle of least privilege, and model outputs are sampled for accuracy, bias, or leakage of sensitive information. Each finding is assigned a severity, an owner, and a remediation date. The final report separates blocking issues from recommendations that can be phased in over time.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: This section of the audit examines who may approve a new AI tool, how training data was obtained, and whether the organization can demonstrate provenance for models and datasets. It checks for rights issues such as copyright infringement, privacy violations, and breach of confidentiality in both inputs and outputs. The audit also reviews incident response procedures, human review of automated decisions, and the terms of vendor agreements against actual usage. It is a factual assessment of controls, not legal advice, and it prepares the organization to answer questions from regulators or opposing counsel. The goal is to show that AI use is deliberate, documented, and reversible when necessary.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: AI enablement audits are moving from periodic project reviews to continuous monitoring embedded in procurement and model registries. As AI-specific case law and enforcement actions accumulate, the audit will draw on live feeds of regulatory changes and contractual precedent. The practice is likely to converge with existing SOC 2, ISO 27001, and privacy audits rather than remain a separate silo. Organizations will increasingly require vendors to provide audit-ready evidence such as model cards, data lineage, and red-team results. The audit will become a standing function of enterprise risk management rather than a one-off consulting engagement.
